To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the attitudes of children hospitalized for asthma are similar to those of adults hospitalized for asthma.
(a) the attitudes of children with chronic asthma can be classified into seven clusters, and (b) these clusters are related to age and to other variables.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and testing of an instrument designed to assess attitudes toward chronic illness.
the development and validation of a set of attitude clusters that are applicable to the hospitalized pediatric patient.
the identification of basic attitudes toward illness and hospitalization in a population of pediatric asthmatic patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the attitude clusters delineated in this study are useful in the understanding of pediatric attitudes toward chronic illness, but that further research is necessary before they can be used as an instrument for clinical assessment and intervention.
attitudes toward chronic illness and hospitalization in childhood are not unitary but are complex and multidimensional.
attitudes toward illness and hospitalization are complex, multidimensional phenomena that are subject to change and that may undergo transformations with the passage of time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the child's hospital experience is an important determinant of attitudes toward chronic illness and the hospital.
the attitude clusters are stable over the short run but changeable over the long term.
the attitudes of children with asthma toward their disease and the hospital are not uniform, but vary widely.
The main takeaway from our work is that
attitudes toward illness or treatment may be stable over long time periods but are also subject to change over shorter time periods.
the attitudes of pediatric patients toward their illness and hospitalization can be reliably measured and are not simply a reflection of parental attitudes.
the patient’s perception of his or her illness and hospitalization may be as important in the healing process as the medical treatment.
